$\{6x - 8y - 31 = 0; 2x - 4y - 6 = 0$

$$
\{6x - 8y - 31 = 0(1); 2x - 4y - 6 = 0(2)
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2x - 4y - 6 &= 0 \\ 2x - 4y &= 6 \\ 2x &= 6 + 4y \\ x &= \dfrac{6 + 4y}{2} \\ x &= 3 + 2y \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=3+2y$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 6x - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 6(3 + 2y) - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 18 + 12y - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ -13 + 4y &= 0 \\ 4y &= 13 \\ y &= \dfrac{13}{4} \end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute

$$
y=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 6x - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 8\left(\dfrac{13}{4}\right) - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 26 - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 57 &= 0 \\ 6x &= 57 \\ x &= \dfrac{19}{2} \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=\dfrac{19}{2}$ and

$$
y=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

, which can be written as

$$
\left(\dfrac{19}{2},\dfrac{13}{4}\right)

The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

$({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}})$
where ${\color{blue}{x}}$ is any number. Consequently, any ${\color{red}{y}}$-value in our solution is *dependent* on a corresponding ${\color{blue}{x}}$-value. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*dependent*.
- Next, we consider the following system:
$\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=2x + 1 \\ y &=1 - x\end{aligned}\right.$
This system has a single solution corresponding to the unique intersection point of the two lines.![](images/bd/bd7edb530e16b853318a3e38785c7b6353c1b54f10ee3c4e2de7da915450f6d9.png)
The unique solution $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ is given by the single point $({\color{blue}{0}},{\color{red}{1}})$. In this case, the components of the solution do not depend on $x$ or $y$. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*independent*.
